timeline.event: Fiddler Moses J. Bonner's family settles in the Dallas area; he reportedly learns fiddle from an older Black fiddler, later moves to Parker County and (1878) Fort Worth.
First Collin County fair held on the site of today's Old Settlers Park, McKinney.
First Texas seven-shape community singing school (Showalter teachers at Giddings); the method later spread statewide.
First Wise County old settlers/Confederate reunion at Cold Springs draws ~5,000; the Messenger reports success, 'only the music being a failure'. Still held each July in Decatur.
Ex-Confederate–Old Settlers' Picnic begins in McKinney (up to 15,000/day in the 1910s–20s; storytelling contests); runs until 1941.
Dallas State Fair (today's State Fair of Texas) chartered.
Fiddler Henry C. Gilliland elected Parker County district clerk (Weatherford).
Approx. 1889–1895: John A. Lomax teaches six years at Weatherford College (Parker County) before entering UT in 1895.
Fort Worth fiddle contest of 19 fiddlers at the UCV Robert E. Lee Camp; Gilliland wins and the Old Fiddlers' Association of Texas is formed.
Armour and Swift packing plants open on Fort Worth's North Side, drawing Czech families
Wise County Old Settlers Association formed.
Sokol KHB Ennis founded by 25 Czech immigrants
Approx.: collecting for Cowboy Songs (1910), Lomax gathers 'Old Chisholm Trail' stanzas in Fort Worth's White Elephant Saloon and 'Git Along, Little Dogies' near Fort Worth.
Dec 29: Texas Folklore Society organized in Dallas at the Texas State Teachers Association meeting (66 members that day).
SPJST Lodge 92 organized in Fort Worth (business in Czech)
Gilliland fiddles at the opening of the State Fair of Texas.
Sons of Hermann Hall (Deep Ellum) completed by German fraternal lodges as a music and dance hall; still active.
Approx.: Blind Lemon Jefferson plays daily at Elm & Central (Deep Ellum/Central Track) and partners with Lead Belly.
'Dallas Blues' (Hart Wand) published, often called the first published blues.
Dallas pianist Alex Moore plays on WRR radio.
Crystal Springs Dance Pavilion opens in Fort Worth (later the cradle of western swing); Knights of Pythias Temple with ballroom opens in Deep Ellum.
Jun 30–Jul 1: Eck Robertson and Parker County fiddler Henry Gilliland record the first commercial country sides for Victor (New York).
Jan 4: WBAP Fort Worth airs the first known radio barn dance, with Confederate-veteran fiddler M. J. Bonner.
Texas Folklore Society publication No. 2, Coffee in the Gourd, published in Dallas by SMU.
John A. Lomax becomes vice president of Republic National Company in Dallas (to 1931).

Dec 3–6: Columbia temporary studio in Deep Ellum records Blind Willie Johnson ('Dark Was the Night', later on the Voyager Golden Record), Coley Jones, and the Dallas String Band's 'Dallas Rag' (Dec 6).
V. O. Stamps moves to Dallas to run Stamps-Baxter's western operations; Columbia returns in December (Dallas String Band Dec 8–9; Blind Willie Johnson Dec 5).

Eck Robertson's family band records for Victor in Dallas (Aug 12; Oct 10–11), including duets with Dr. J. B. Cranfill; Bob Wills moves to Fort Worth and first records (Brunswick, Dallas); T-Bone Walker cuts 'Wichita Falls Blues' in Dallas; Coley Jones records 'Drunkard's Special' (Child 274).
Interstate Sacred Harp Convention at Mineral Wells (just west of the MSA); president W. H. Coston of Dallas; observed by George Pullen Jackson.
Wills Fiddle Band (Wills, Arnspiger, Milton and Derwood Brown) wins a fiddle contest, broadcasts on KFJZ and WBAP and plays Crystal Springs.
Light Crust Doughboys formed in Fort Worth (Burrus Mill sponsorship).
Old Fiddlers Reunion begins in Athens (just outside the MSA); 94th edition in 2025.
Milton Brown forms the Musical Brownies, the 'first western swing band', based at Crystal Springs; Cecil Brower and Jesse Ashlock create the twin-fiddle sound.
Lone Star Cowboys (Shelton Brothers and Leon Chappelear) record the first 'Deep Elm Blues'.
Texas Quality Network (WBAP, WFAA, WOAI, KPRC, KOMA) formed, largely to share Doughboys broadcasts.
Don Law's first field sessions at 508 Park Avenue, Dallas, including the first Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys records; Sportatorium opens Dec 9.
Stamps quartets begin a daily noonday program on KRLD Dallas; the Carter Quartet (later the Chuck Wagon Gang) is on WBAP Fort Worth.
Milton Brown dies (Apr 18) after a car crash; up to 3,500 attend his funeral. The Stamps Quartet's noonday KRLD show begins in the fall.
June: three-week session at 508 Park records Robert Johnson's last sides (Jun 19–20), Bob Wills, Light Crust Doughboys and Black Boy Shine.
Stamps-Baxter All Night Singing in the Cotton Bowl, broadcast internationally on KRLD.
National Hall built on Roberts Cut-Off Rd, Fort Worth
Final 508 Park session (conjunto: Lolo Cavazos, Hermanas Fraga, Gaytán y Cantú); 843 recordings made there from 1935 to 1939.
Eck Robertson records about 100 fiddle tunes at Jack Sellers' studio in Dallas (now lost); V. O. Stamps dies in Dallas.
Last Collin County Old Settlers picnic; Dec 9–10: Library of Congress man-on-the-street recordings made in Dallas after Pearl Harbor.
Big D Jamboree debuts on KRLD on Oct 16 (grew from the 1946 Texas State Barn Dance); up to 5,000 weekly at the Sportatorium until 1966.
Major Franklin (Whitewright/Grayson Co.) wins the world fiddle championship at Crockett.
TIFD's Texas Camp (international folk dance) begins.
Johnny Gimble settles in Dallas (Big D Jamboree; Boyd brothers).
Dallas lawyer-folklorist Hermes Nye releases Anglo-American Ballads on Folkways (more LPs through 1959).
Hermes Nye's Texas Folk Songs on Folkways (introduction by J. Frank Dobie).
1955–57: Benny Thomasson, a Dallas auto-body worker, wins the Crockett World Championship three years running.
Indian Relocation Act of 1956; Dallas was a designated relocation city in the 1950s; >20,000 Native Americans moved to DFW by 1970
Jan 24: Rubaiyat opens at 3133 McKinney Ave, Texas's first folk club; Dallas Folk Music Society co-founded (Lu Mitchell, Hermes Nye circle).
Stagecoach Ballroom opens in Fort Worth (Oct); Harvest Holiday round-dance festival begins (inferred from the 66th edition in 2026).
Scottish Society of Dallas organized.
Approximate start of the annual DFW powwow later held at Traders Village (54th in 2016; inferred)
Folk Music Club founded at North Texas State (Denton) by Stan Alexander (Fromholz, Murphey, Hubbard); Panther Hall opens in Fort Worth.
Jerry Jeff Walker arrives at the Rubaiyat; later debuts 'Mr. Bojangles' there.
County Records issues 'Texas Fiddle Favorites' with Major and Louis Franklin and Kaufman County's Norman Solomon.
Big D Jamboree ends; Crystal Springs pavilion burns (Dec); the National Polka Festival is first organized in Ennis per TSHA (the festival itself gives 1967).
Anita N. Martinez elected to Dallas City Council; Fort Worth Greek Festival begins (inferred from 57th in 2025)
Rubaiyat sold and moved to Maple Ave (manager Allen Damron); Texas International Pop Festival at Lewisville.
Texas Old Time Fiddlers Association founded; Bob Wills's last session (For the Last Time) recorded in Dallas.
Southwest Bluegrass Club founded (50th anniversary 2024).
The Rubaiyat (by then on Maple St, managed by Allen Damron) closes; Stamps-Baxter sold to Zondervan.
Anita N. Martinez Ballet Folklórico and Ballet Folklórico Azteca de Fort Worth founded
Poor David's Pub opens on McKinney Ave (March 15).
Panther Hall (Fort Worth country dance hall, Cowtown Jamboree TV) closes.
Brave Combo forms in Denton.
Scarborough Faire first run in Waxahachie.
Uncle Calvin's Coffee House founded by Rev. Trey Hammond (NorthPark Presbyterian).
KNON community radio goes on air (July 30) with afternoon folk blocks and the Texas Folk Music Show.
Feb 12: first public contra dance (Irving, Lone Star State Dulcimer Society); Mar 5: 'First Texas Céilí' at Nick Farrelly's, the start of the North Texas Irish Festival.
Vietnamese American Community of Greater Dallas founded
NTIF moves to Fair Park; Southwest Celtic Music Association formed; contras move to Winfrey Point (White Rock Lake).

About this year the annual Sacred Harp singings at Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary and the Dallas County Singing begin (inferred from their numbering). KNON's first Texas Music Celebration at Sons of Hermann Hall (Oct 5), during the Saturday Songwriter's Sanctuary era.
Green Belt Rappers (rapper sword) debut at the Christmas dance.
Winfrey Belles Morris debut at a maypole dance (May 3); North Texas Traditional Dance Society incorporated (May 15); the film "Square Dance" (1987) is shot at the Stagecoach Ballroom, Fort Worth.
NTTDS becomes a CDSS associate; first MayFaire.
Dallas Songwriters Association formally established (independent nonprofit 1990).
Texas Scottish Festival & Highland Games first held at Caelum Moor, Arlington (June; another source says 1986); Addison Oktoberfest begins (approx.).
Alex Moore named NEA National Heritage Fellow, the first African-American Texan so honored.
Poor David's starts the B.W. Stevenson Memorial Songwriting Contest.
Dallas Kiyari Daiko taiko group forms
Red Steagall Cowboy Gathering founded at Cowtown Coliseum (34th in 2025).
First NTTDS spring contra weekend (named When in Doubt, Swing! in 1992).
Monthly English country dance begins at SMU; Dallas Highland Dancers founded.

Cowtown Opry organized (Nov 2), from an idea by Stockyards Hotel pianist Jean Marlowe Keim; one source dates the formal club to 1995; Buckaroo youth club 1997; at the Livestock Exchange Building since 2001.
Johnny Gimble named NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Light Crust Doughboys named official music ambassadors of Texas; Denton contra dances begin (to 2003); approximate first Deep Ellum Arts Festival.
First UTA NASA powwow (inferred from 29th in 2025)
Dondoko Taiko founded in Fort Worth with Nagaoka sister city support
First New Year's Fiddler's Dream music and dance camp at Cross Point Camp (Lake Texoma).
Death of Jim O'Flaherty, Irish immigrant host of North Texas house sessions.
Denton Irish session starts at Banter; Oct 13: Ken Fleming launches the Sunday session players at Trinity Hall, Dallas.
Tipperary Inn, Dallas's main session pub, closes; the session moves to Trinity Hall.
Sportatorium demolished.
First O'Flaherty Irish Music Retreat (October).
Poor David's moves to the Cedars (Guy Clark opens the room); Eric Clapton films at 508 Park.
TIMES founded (January); J. Gilligan's Tuesday session begins in Arlington after O'Dwyer's in Euless is sold.
Clarence Teng converts the Plaza Theater, Carrollton, into a dance hall; contras there until 2016.
Ennis Czech Music Festival and IIAmericas Celebration begin (inferred)
Valerie Ryals (Burleson) becomes the first woman fiddler in the Texas Fiddlers Hall of Fame; Dallas Folk Music Society marks its 50th anniversary.
The Kessler Theater (once owned by Gene Autry) reopens as a music venue in Oak Cliff.
Dallas-born, Rockwall-based Jim "Texas Shorty" Chancellor named NEA National Heritage Fellow; NTTDS hosts its first Set for Spring English country dance weekend; Fiddler's Dream passes to NTTDS.
North Texas School of Irish Music started; Paluxy River Bluegrass Association founded.
Fort Worth contra dance started by Ellie Hayes (~50 at the first dance); discontinued Oct 2016.
Dallas Hua Yun Chinese Orchestra founded; Cowtown Conjunto Festival begins (inferred)
Pegasus Squares (IAGSDC) founded.
TIMES Session Players begin Sundays at The Celt, McKinney.
Approx.: Bob Wills Fiddle Festival & Contest begins in Greenville (11th annual in 2025).
Texas state mariachi contest begins (became official UIL contest 2020)
Last Irving contra dance (Dec); Texas Scottish Festival reportedly moves from Arlington to Decatur (medium confidence).
Lu Mitchell, 'godmother of Dallas folk', dies at 95.
First FWSSR Fiddle Showdown (6th annual in 2025); Trinity Hall pub closes in the pandemic (2021).
UTD students form Contra Corners (Feb); all NTTDS dances cancelled for COVID (Mar).
COVID: Uncle Calvin's goes dark (never re-listed shows); Dallas County Sacred Harp singing pauses 2020-2021.
J. Gilligan's session suspended (Sept); Malarkey's session ended after BMI licensing threat; Staggering-Irishman-era sessions cancelled.
ICAE Native American Heritage Month Powwow and Cowtown Birthplace of Western Swing Festival begin
39th North Texas Irish Festival held virtually; UTD dances resume outdoors.

NTTDS contras resume at the 2155 Ballroom, Carrollton (Mar), now 3rd Saturdays only; English country dance resumes (Oct); Fort Worth Scottish country dance class begins (Oct 1); NTIF returns in person.
River of the Canoes Powwow at Dallas City Hall Plaza (AIHDT 10th anniversary)
Bluegrass Heritage Foundation takes up Lester Flatt's 1942 Martin D-18 #81197.
NTTDS adopts pay-what-you-can admission (May).
The Texas Scottish Festival was reportedly last scheduled for May 2024 (unverified); a new Decatur Celtic Festival used the same fairgrounds in May 2025.

When in Doubt, Swing! resumes (Apr); Ron Shipman dies (May 2) and his Rubaiyat archive goes to the Wittliff Collections; City of Dallas takes over Old City Park (May 27); Fort Worth Songwriter Fest founded; Zounds Sounds B-Side opens; Southwest Bluegrass Club turns 50 with the first Grape Jam (Oct).
Rizes Hellenic Dance Festival founded (Jan, Fort Worth); African American Dance Caller Pathways launched (Sept).
Traders Village GP replaces its powwow with 'A Gathering at the Village'; first Big D Bhangra Competition; Dallas Zydeco & Southern Soul fest at City Hall

Fiddler's Dream New Year camp resumes (Jan); NTTDS English country dance moves to Ridgewood Park UMC (spring); DFW singings adopt The Sacred Harp: 2025 Edition; Bluegrass Heritage Foundation starts a monthly show & jam at Poor David's Pub.

Anita N. Martinez dies at 100 (Apr 10); the UTA powwow holds its 30th edition (Apr 4); Ennis celebrates 60 years of the National Polka Festival (May); Dirty Job Brewing (Mansfield session) closes and the Henry McCarty session opens in Fort Worth (May); David Card hands Poor David's to his daughter Amelia (Jun 1); the National Square Dance Convention meets in Waco (June).

City-funded son jarocho workshops in East Dallas (Jul-Sep); NTIF announces it will leave Fair Park for Denton (Aug); NTTDS ends pay-what-you-can and returns to $10 admission (Aug); North Texas Pow Wow at Esports Stadium Arlington (Oct 24); Granada Theater announces it will close in April 2027 (Oct 30).
North Texas Irish Festival moves from Fair Park to Denton (Mar 13-14).

costs.notes: Every session and jam found is free. Irish pubs often comp musicians (Gillespie's: one free drink; Henry McCarty: meal and validated parking; Granbury: food and drinks). Dallas old-time jam: an instrument gets you into the park free; non-playing companions used to pay about $5. BHF Poor David's show & jam: free with tip jar. SWBC 'O Brother' night: $15, or $20 a couple. O'Flaherty Youth Camp: $120. Wernick jam class: $300. State banjo/guitar/mandolin championship entry: $20-25. NTTDS contra: $10 adult / $5 student or child / $25 family (fixed since Aug 2026; pay-what-you-can May 2023-Aug 2026; first dance in 1983 was a $1 donation). UTD student contra and AADCP dances are free. Sacred Harp singings and Cowtown Opry shows are free. Dan's Silverleaf songwriter open mic: no cover. Listening-room tickets about $20 (Opening Bell; Dallas Songwriter Festival 2025). Poor David's songwriting contest entry $30. House-concert prices are not published. Heritage events are mostly free: powwows (UTA, North Texas, ICAE: free), Fort Worth Greek Festival, Lebanese festival, Día de los Muertos parades, Fiestas Patrias. Paid: Texas Mariachi Festival $60-150; Tejano Fest $30; Ukrainian Christmas show $75; zydeco line-dance fest $20-35; Israeli dance about $5/session; West African drum class $20; FW Fall Japanese Festival $15 adult. Stagecoach Ballroom: about $8-9 cover (search summary, unverified).

surprises: The first radio barn dance was in Fort Worth: WBAP, Jan 4, 1923, with 75-year-old Confederate-veteran fiddler M. J. Bonner playing square-dance tunes, two years before the Grand Ole Opry (TSHA: WBAP).

A Dallas field recording is in interstellar space: Blind Willie Johnson cut "Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground" in a temporary Columbia studio in Deep Ellum on Dec 3, 1927, and it flies on the Voyager Golden Record.

Texas's first folk club was in Dallas, not Austin: the 30-seat Rubaiyat (Jan 1959) had the state's only espresso machine, borrowed chairs from Jack Ruby, and a founder who sang sea shanties standing on a barrel. Today the 8.5-million-person metro has no shanty sing at all (D Magazine, Apr 2025).

Half of the first country record (1922) was Henry Gilliland, a former Parker County district clerk who had won the 1901 Fort Worth contest that founded the Old Fiddlers' Association of Texas; a former Prohibition Party vice-presidential nominee, Dr. J. B. Cranfill, fiddled duets on Eck Robertson's 1929 Dallas Victor session.

The father of modern Texas contest fiddling, Benny Thomasson, worked in a Dallas auto-body shop and later moved to Washington state; Hall of Famer Norman Solomon put in 40 years at General Dynamics. Texas style grew partly as a Metroplex blue-collar art.
Eck Robertson recorded about 100 fiddle tunes at a Dallas transcription studio in 1940. They have never surfaced and not even a tune list survives.

DFW contra was born inside a dulcimer club (Irving, Feb 12, 1983, $1 donation). The fourth-largest US metro now has exactly one adult community contra a month, in a Carrollton strip-mall ballroom, while NORTEX lists 25 square and round dance clubs and Fort Worth's Swingtime Center will not rent to anyone but square-dance clubs through 2027.

DFW has run an invited, rotated, published-roster "session players" institution since Oct 13, 2002 (Trinity Hall, then The Celt in McKinney): a curated pub performance session that sits beside about 17 open Irish sessions a month.

Venues die, musicians don't: the Denton Irish session is 24 years old and has lived in five venues, and a Dallas slow session lost its pub when BMI agents threatened the bar over a missing live-music license.

The bluegrass scene is a daytime one: jams at 10:30am on a Thursday in a public library, in senior centers and church halls, and in a winery inside a 1945 post office. Meanwhile the lone Dallas old-time jam's rules explicitly bar bluegrass.

Fort Worth is training Black square and contra callers: African American Dance Caller Pathways (2025) teaches the African American roots of calling, and its free dances are the only squares or contras in Fort Worth proper since 2016.

A Southern Baptist seminary has hosted an annual Sacred Harp singing since about 1985, founded by hymnologist William J. Reynolds and now led by his son; Dallas was also the capital of seven-shape gospel publishing (Stamps-Baxter), which broadcast all-night singings from the Cotton Bowl, yet no seven-shape convention singing survives in the metro.

A Czech lodge hall built in 1938 by North Side meatpacking families (National Hall, SPJST #92) is now the home of Fort Worth's "Birthplace of Western Swing" festival and of Tejano dances, and the Czech-authenticity National Polka Festival in Ennis is headlined by Denton polka-rock band Brave Combo.

The Fort Worth Stock Show pays teenage fiddlers $7,500 in scholarships and also hosts high-school mariachi and youth escaramuza championships; Grand Prairie ISD starts mariachi in 6th grade, which probably makes mariachi the metro's largest youth violin tradition.

One of America's oldest Irish festivals began as the "First Texas Ceili" in a bar (Nick Farrelly's, Mar 5, 1983) and is leaving Fair Park for the Denton fairgrounds in 2027; and the NEA's own bio of Rockwall fiddler Texas Shorty credits him with Thomasson's 1955-57 three-peat, when he was 12.
curiosities: Contra density: DFW has about 0.12-0.24 contra dances a month per million people. How does that compare across the 20 metros, and why is the Sun Belt's largest metro so thin?
Did COVID permanently halve contra frequency in Sun Belt metros (DFW went from about 2.25 to 1 a month) while New England series came back at full strength?
What is the ratio of modern-Western square-dance nights to contra nights in each metro? Is DFW's roughly 10:1 typical of the South and Midwest?
Why is old-time nearly absent in DFW while bluegrass is strong? Is the same true in Houston, Atlanta and Phoenix, and does Texas contest fiddling fill the old-time niche?
Does any other metro have an invited, rotated "session players" institution like TIMES's, and how do curated performance sessions affect open sessions?
How many students play in school mariachis in DFW versus Houston, San Antonio, Phoenix and Los Angeles? Is mariachi now the largest youth fiddle tradition in Sun Belt metros?

Sacred Harp per capita: DFW has about 3.7 singings a month and no weekly singing, while much smaller Austin has one. Which metros have institution-hosted annual singings (seminaries, universities), and do they sustain local singing?
Why do some metros of 8 million have no shanty sing or ballad circle (DFW, apparently Houston) while small cities do? Is it a Sun Belt, Texas, or car-centered-metro pattern?

Among 1950s BIA relocation cities (Dallas, Denver, LA, Chicago, Minneapolis, Seattle, the Bay Area, Phoenix), which still have weekly or monthly drum or gourd-dance practice open to the community, and which have only annual powwows?

Are Czech, German and other fraternal halls in other metros (Houston SPJST lodges, Chicago and Cleveland Sokols) surviving by becoming western-swing, Tejano or general dance venues, as National Hall has?
Are legacy urban heritage festivals leaving historic fairgrounds for exurban ones (NTIF: Fair Park to Denton), and what happens to attendance and the session/dance content when they do?
Is a metro's folk memory usually archived inside it? DFW's Rubaiyat, Panther Hall and western swing collections sit 200 miles away in San Marcos.
How common are Black caller-training programs like AADCP (cf. Chicago's Southside Squares), and do they change who comes to community dances?
Do other metros have a church-hall coffeehouse lineage like Uncle Calvin's (Presbyterian, 1982) and Martin's Music Cafe (Lutheran), and did COVID end more of these than commercial rooms?
data_quality_notes:
Method: five research threads (sessions, dance, song, heritage, history) on Oct 30, 2026, using web search and direct fetches only; merged and deduplicated by hand. web_search was rate-limited in the history thread, and tunearch.org, loc.gov, TARO and UNT ArchivesSpace blocked automated fetches, so the TTA tune details ("Dallas Rag", "Dallas Bound") come from search snippets and no Lomax/WPA field recordings made in DFW could be confirmed (only the LOC Dec 1941 man-on-the-street recordings).

Coverage: Irish sessions (thesession.org API plus comment threads, TIMES, pub calendars), Sacred Harp (two independent 2026 directories agree) and the NTTDS dance world (2026 newsletters) are strong. Bluegrass rests on the undated Southwest Bluegrass Club jam list cross-checked against Facebook, Meetup and allevents posts; aggregators (StartJamming, Jamfinder) garble days. Facebook-only groups were often unreadable, so suburban jams, gospel quartet anniversaries, house concerts and temple-based South Asian activity are undercounted; heritage totals are a verified floor.

Weak or unverified items: the Dallas Old-Time Music Jam (standing listings only; newest dated event 2019; park changed operators May 2024), Hooligan's first-Sunday session (May 2024), Times Ten Cellars and Mid-Cities bluegrass jams (low), Denton Irish session frequency (2nd and 4th vs 2nd Saturday only), RikuDallas venue (Beth Torah vs JCC), Dallas Aztec Dancers (low), Cowtown Pickers jam (Aug 2025), Stagecoach Ballroom schedule (undated site; a Sept 2026 listing found in a merger spot-check), Cowtown Opry (own site stale; Stockyards page current). The 12 NORTEX clubs without published schedules are not counted, so square_dance (11/month) understates an estimated 20-35 club dances a month.

Totals: recurring_events_per_month_total counts in-MSA participatory series with 2024-26 evidence, including annual heritage gatherings at 0.083/month. Excluded (see recurring_events_excluded_from_totals): 11 bar blues jams (about 48/month from bluesdfw.com, Dec 2025), round dancing, Lindy swing at Sons of Hermann Hall, the invited TIMES Session Players (4.33/month), Martin's Music Cafe concerts, spectator festivals, and two series without 2024-26 evidence (Dallas Slow Sessions; Dallas Acoustic Song Circle). Poor David's Monday open mic is counted only for its monthly in-person night. Including blues jams and the invited session the total would be about 52 a month higher. festivals_active includes some multi-genre festivals with folk stages (Wildflower!, Deep Ellum Arts Festival, Scarborough Faire, Addison Oktoberfest) and annual contests.

distinct_traditions_active = 39: 16 layer 1-3 traditions plus 23 heritage traditions with verified 2024-26 activity; the list is in headline_stats.distinct_traditions_active_note. It excludes traditions seen only before 2024 (Korean pungmul, 2023) or only name-checked (klezmer, Filipino rondalla, Scandinavian, Vietnamese traditional music).

Contradictions resolved: (1) Norman Solomon and Orville Burns: the history thread found no DFW tie, but fiddlersfrolics.org (confirmed by a merger spot-check) gives Solomon's Kaufman County birth and 40 years at General Dynamics, and Burns is buried in Fort Worth. (2) National Polka Festival founding: 1966 (TSHA) vs 1967 (festival); recorded as 1967 with a note. (3) Texas Scottish Festival founding: 1986 vs June 1987 at Caelum Moor; status is hiatus (site said "2025 TBA" in Apr 2026); a merger spot-check found only a separately named, self-described new Decatur Celtic Festival at the same fairgrounds on May 2-3, 2025. (4) William J. Reynolds Sacred Harp singing numbering: 1995 minutes imply a 1985 start (2025 = 41st) but 2025 minutes say 39th; missing years likely explain it. (5) Coppell singing address 420 vs 425 S Heartz Rd. (6) Greek Food Festival of Dallas edition: 70th, 71st or 72nd. (7) Ballet Folklorico Azteca founding 1974 vs 1975. (8) Uncle Calvin's seats 200 vs 220; dormant since about 2020 (no closure announcement). (9) Cowtown Opry organized Nov 2, 1992 (its history page) vs a 1995 club date in one thread's notes. (10) Texas Shorty: born in Dallas (NEA), living in Rockwall (2010 press); the NEA bio wrongly gives him Thomasson's 1955-57 three-peat. (11) Bob Wills Fiddle Festival contest venue: The Landmark on Lee (2026 TOTFA listing) vs the Texan Theater. (12) The "36th annual" Traders Village powwow (Nov 2026) is in Houston, not Grand Prairie; Grand Prairie's September powwow (54th in 2016) seems to have lapsed. (13) Stamps-Baxter All Night Singing: 1936 (history thread) vs "by 1938" (TSHA gospel entry); timeline uses 1938. (14) contradancelinks.com still lists a Fort Worth contra that ended in 2016.

Not found (not the same as absent): any Scottish/Cape Breton, Scandinavian, Balkan, klezmer, gypsy-jazz or French-Canadian session; any public ceili or set dance; any morris, sword or rapper team since the 1980s sides; any shanty sing or ballad circle; any seven-shape convention singing in the 11 counties; a Comhaltas branch; a DFW folk podcast or label; NTTDS and NORTEX membership counts; Ennis halls' year-round public dances; school mariachi student counts; current Texas Scottish Festival dates.
nutshell: DFW is where recorded Texas folk music was born, and today its scene lives mostly in suburbs, church halls and once-a-year gatherings. Fort Worth gave the world the first radio barn dance (1923), western swing (1931-32) and the 1901 contest that founded Texas's first fiddlers' association; Benny Thomasson rebuilt the Texas contest style while working in a Dallas body shop. Now bluegrass is the biggest jam culture (about 18 jams a month, mostly daytime, in churches, senior centers, a library and town squares), Irish music is the best organized (about 15 open sessions a month, largely coordinated by TIMES), and Sacred Harp singers meet almost weekly in four rotating towns. Old-time is nearly absent and contra has shrunk to one monthly dance, while modern Western square-dance clubs outnumber it about ten to one. The largest living traditions are Mexican-American (school mariachi, folklorico, matachines), Texas Czech polka in Ennis, intertribal powwows and Navratri garba.
